title: Chapter 222 – Tied Threads
html:
[Terrace Six – Jian]

Jian takes the loom beside Pebble's, because nobody else will, and because he has decided that if he is going to be shown the end of his life he would like it to be in good company.

The frame is the same: squat, dark, patient. The shuttle is the same pale ash. The spool beside the beam is a different color, though, a pale grayish blue that he does not remember choosing, and when he lifts it the thread slides over his fingers with a faint cool tingle, like water. He sets it in the pin. He passes the shuttle through the warp for the first time.

The young weaver with glass-bead eyes is standing at his elbow. Corin, Tamsin called him. He has been standing there for a quarter of an hour, with his hands loose at his sides, and in that time he has not blinked once.

"I do not need you," Jian says gently.

Corin does not move.

"I know how to weave. I have done it before." It is not strictly true. He has watched a thousand hands at a thousand looms, in the memory of another man's life, and he knows the motion as one knows a dance seen only through a window. "You may go and sit."

The glass eyes turn toward him. For one moment, something moves behind them, a flicker, a ripple, like a fish under ice. Then it is gone, and Corin bows, and walks away down the long row with the soft unhurried step of a man who has not been asked to do anything for three hundred years and has no idea what to do with the freedom.

Jian watches him go.

That will be me, he thinks. If I stay.

He turns back to the loom.

---

The first hours go by in ordinary light.

He sees the rain on a window, in a city he can no longer name. He sees a laboratory at three in the morning, a bank of screens, a half-eaten sandwich going stale on a steel desk. He sees his own hands, the other man's hands, Ethan Cole's long clever ones, soldering a connector no bigger than a grain of rice. He sees a woman's face in a doorway, backlit, saying something he cannot hear. He sees a hospital corridor, a white ceiling, a clock.

The thread lays itself down in the weave, thin and gray-blue and fine as hair.

It starts in the wrong place, he thinks, dimly.

He had expected the cloth to begin with a Lin birth. A cradle, a courtyard, a clan with a well in the middle. But the first inch of the ribbon is another man's life, and it is only at the second hand's-breadth that the weave shifts, and darkens, and a different color enters the warp: a warm, dull, tawny brown, like wet earth.

It is a boy's life. It is a life of a boy of nine who has just woken in a bed that is not his own, in a body that is not his own, in a house that smells of cedar and sickness. It is the first night. He remembers that night with a clarity so absolute that it goes through him like a nail. He remembers lying very still and listening to the sound of an unfamiliar heart. He remembers thinking, quite calmly: I have been given a second chance. I must not waste it.

I wasted it, he thinks. I wasted it on being useful.

The shuttle passes. The thread lays down.

He sees the clan, the Council, the first lie. He sees the first time he spoke to the machine and it answered in a voice that was almost kind. He sees the Mending: nine hands laid on a stone table, and the days going out of them like threads out of a spool. He sees Mei, white-haired at sixty-four. He sees Mo Yan at the Quay, with a black glass bell, saying Mama to the dark.

It is not a pleasant weave. It is not meant to be.

He keeps going.

---

On the fourth hour, the cloth begins to show him the future.

He knows it at once, by the way the colors change. The tawny brown runs out, and the weave goes thin and fast, and the thread that lays itself down is no longer gray-blue but a hard bright silver, the color of a sword. It is the color of a thing that has not happened yet. It runs through the warp like a fault in glass.

He sees the Sixth Terrace. He sees the Seventh, a long gray plain under a rolling sky. He sees the Eighth. He sees Hua, with a thread of white in her hair, speaking to a woman in the mist. He sees Pebble, a boy no longer, tall and grave. He sees Veyra Thann standing at the foot of a great white stair with her hood thrown back.

Then he sees the room.

He knows it already; Pebble has described it to him in a low shaking voice, an hour ago, at the water cistern. A high round chamber, white as bone. A roof of pale glass. A floor of pale stone, and in the middle of it a ring of nine seats, deep and narrow, each carved from a single block. He sees himself walk into it. He sees himself in a plain gray robe with a hand outstretched, and he knows it is his own, because the hand does not shake.

He sees the seats fill.

There is Hua, small and upright, with the Warden's mark on her palm. There is Yue, her stone hand open on her knee. There is Han, white-bearded, enormous, with his sword across his lap. There is Hai Ren with her scrolls and Cheng Hui with his dry smile; there is Tian Mo, grown gray at the temples; there is a woman with silver hair and a stick who he knows, with a pang, is Mei. There is a girl he does not know at the far side of the ring, nine years old, in a cloak too long for her, with a white bell in her lap.

Eight seats. Nine seats.

The ninth is empty.

He stands in the center of the ring with the glass roof above him and the Seam beyond, a long pale scar across the dark. He lifts his hand. He says a word he cannot hear.

The seats light.

It is the most beautiful thing he has ever seen. A ring of nine lights, each a different color, each pulsing with a different heart. He feels the Print wake in him like a long-sleeping dog. He feels the Ring close. He feels the strangest lightness, the lifting of an unbearable weight, as though a man who had carried a mountain on his back for a thousand years had at last been allowed to put it down.

And then, very quietly, in the silence that follows, the thread ends.

---

The shuttle falls from his fingers.

He sits on the stool, with his hand open on his knee and the loom ticking down around him. The cloth is spooled in his lap. It is a narrow ribbon, gray-blue and tawny-brown and bright silver, and it ends, at the length of his forearm, in a clean sharp edge, as though cut with a blade.

He looks at it.

There is no more. The thread does not go on. It does not fade, as Pebble's red cord faded into some unimaginable distance. It does not blur into mist. It simply stops, at the moment the nine lights come on, as a sentence stops at a full point.

I die there, he thinks.

It is not a surprise. It is a click, a small cold settling, like a key turning in a well-oiled lock. He has known it, he realizes, for a long time. Since the Hall of Ten Thousand Names. Since the Mending. Since the day he first saw the Ring leak and understood that a machine built to share a burden among nine would, in the end, need nine to bear it, and that one of the nine would be the one who could not be replaced.

Of course it is me, he thinks. I am the one who is holding the thread.

A small dry cough sounds at his shoulder.

"You have finished," says Tamsin.

He does not look up.

"How long?" he says.

"Six hours of the Terrace. Almost a year of the world." The old Keeper's voice is mild. "I have never seen anyone weave so fast. You did not stop once."

"I did not want to."

"No." A pause. "I did not think you would."

She stands beside him, tall and white and calm, with her sewn eyes turned toward the cloth. Her fingers drift down, lightly, and touch the end of the ribbon. She reads it as a blind woman reads a face.

"It is a short one," she says.

"I know."

"It is shorter than most." She lifts her hand. "I am sorry."

"Don't be."

"I always am. It is a thing I cannot help." A faint, wry smile. "You are a man who looks at an ending and says of course. I have only ever met one other."

"Orrin."

"Orrin." She nods. "You are much alike. It is a pity. He was a good man."

---

Jian finds Yue at her loom an hour later.

She has been at it for a long time. She sits with her back as straight as a spear, her stone hand resting on the beam and her right hand passing the shuttle, and there is a look on her face that he has seen only once before, in the tower of the Wall, on the night the Elder died. It is the look of someone doing a very difficult thing with great precision, so as not to feel it.

He sits down on the next stool. He does not speak.

The shuttle goes across. The harness lifts. The thread lays down.

After a while she says, without turning her head, "I saw you."

"Saw me?"

"In the cloth. At the end." The shuttle passes. "I was weaving the last years. I saw the white room, and the nine seats. I saw you walk in. I saw you stand in the middle." Her voice is level. "I saw the lights come on."

"Yes."

"I saw you go out."

"Yes."

"Then I saw myself." The shuttle pauses. "Four seats along. In a gray cloak. Sitting upright with my stone hand open on my knee. And when the lights came on, I did not move." She draws a breath. "I did not move, Jian. I sat there while the whole ring went white, and I did not get up."

He says nothing.

"I thought it was a mistake," says Yue. "I thought the Loom had got it wrong. I thought it showed me what I would do if I were weak. If I sat down and let the thing happen and did not try to stop it." Her jaw works. "But it isn't. It's not a mistake. It's the shape of the weave. We end in the same hour."

"We are tied."

"We're tied." She says it flatly. "I don't know when. I don't know how. Some time in the last year, in the Orchard or on the stair or in the dark, my thread went round yours and held. I didn't mean it to." Her mouth twists. "I don't mean most things."

"I'm sorry."

"For what? It's my thread."

"It is mine, too."

"Then we're both fools." She turns, at last, and the look in her eyes is dry and bright and entirely without self-pity. "I can see it, you know. Two lengths of cloth, running side by side. One of them gray-blue, one of them red, no, not red, a hard dark gold. They go up the Road together. They go through the Seventh and the Eighth. They go to the Door. And at the Door they go out like a pair of candles in the same draft."

"There's a way to cut it."

She goes still.

"Tamsin told me," Jian says. He keeps his voice low. "While I was finishing. She said a tied thread can be cut. She said she keeps a pair of shears in the north beam, and that no one has asked for them in a hundred years."

"Cut it how?"

"Cleanly. The one who cuts loses nothing. But the one who is cut free—" He swallows. "The one who is cut free loses the tie. Which means they lose the other's life. Not the death. The life." A breath. "A thread that has been tied for a year cannot be cut without taking a year with it."

"A year of whose?"

"The one who holds the shears."

Yue is silent.

It is the silence of a woman who has understood something she has been trying not to understand. She sets down the shuttle. She lays her hands in her lap, the warm and the stone, and looks at them for a long time, as though she had never seen them before.

"So I can cut it," she says. "At the price of a year. And you'll live."

"I'll still die."

"At the Door."

"At the Door. In the white room. But not with you." He holds her gaze. "I will not ask it of you."

"You're not asking."

"I am telling you that it exists. That is all."

"That's what asking is," says Yue. "Don't be a coward, Jian. You've never been any good at it."

---

Tamsin brings Veyra the old cloth in the hour before the meal.

Jian sees it from the stove, where he has gone to warm his hands. The Keeper comes down the long row of looms with a small flat chest of pale wood in her arms, walking by touch, unerring, the ring of her staff on the boards as steady as a clock. She stops before the hooded woman, who is standing alone at the edge of the platform, and holds out the chest.

"I kept it," she says. "I have never opened it. I thought you might wish to."

What is it?

"His first thread. The one he wove in the week before the Door." The sewn eyes are turned toward the hood. "I put it away. I told myself it was for safekeeping. I think I knew, even then, that it was waiting for somebody."

Veyra does not move. The ruined hand, bandaged, lifts from her breastbone and hovers over the lid.

You told me you never asked him what he saw.

"I did not. But I was careful to keep what he made." Tamsin sets the chest in her hands. "A thread is a thing of its own. It does not require an owner's permission to be read. Only a reader."

The hooded woman holds the chest for a long time.

Jian does not mean to watch. He turns back to the stove, and his hands, and the fire. But he cannot help hearing the soft dry click of the latch, or the sigh of the lid, or the rustle of fine cloth being unfolded, and when he glances over his shoulder a moment later Veyra is kneeling on the boards with a narrow white ribbon spread across her knees.

It is not long. It is not longer than his own. It runs a little past her forearm, white and brown and a deep dark green, and at its end there is a place where the weave changes, where a second thread, thin, pale, the color of river water, comes in from the side and lies down against the first.

That is mine, says Veyra.

Her voice is very quiet.

I did not know I was in it. She lays a finger on the place where the two threads meet. I was not there when he wove it. I was across the Terrace, with the other Founders, arguing about the shape of the Door. I never saw him sit down. A breath. And yet here I am, in his cloth, tied to his end.

"He wove you in," says Tamsin.

He wove his future.

"It is the same thing, when you are Orrin." The Keeper's smile is faint. "He could not see his own death, he told you. That was true. He could see only yours. And he saw that yours was bound to his."

Veyra bows her head.

For a time no one speaks. The looms clatter, far away. The stove ticks. Jian has the odd, painful sense of having walked into a room where two people are mourning one another, and the room is very small.

He never told me, says Veyra, at last.

"No."

He knew we would end together. He knew it at the beginning. And he let me think— She stops. He let me think he had sent me to sleep to spare me.

"Perhaps he did."

He sent me to sleep because he could not bear to watch me die at the Door. The cool voice shakes, once, and steadies. He bought me six hundred years. It was the only coin he had.

"And now you have spent them."

Yes.

"Was it worth it?"

Veyra lifts her head. The hood falls back, and in the silver light her face is bare: gray, fine, old, with eyes like river water and a mouth that has forgotten how to smile. She looks, Jian thinks, like a woman who has just been handed a letter she has waited six centuries to open, and has found that it says only I am sorry.

I do not know, she says. Ask me at the Door.

---

They tell the others at the evening meal, because Veyra has said that a thing like this cannot be kept.

Tamsin has laid out bread and cheese on the iron stove's low table, and a jug of the lavender tea. Hua sits cross-legged on the boards with her cloth in her lap. It is the shortest of all. It ends not at the Door but a hand's breadth before it, in a place she will not describe, and she has said only that it is the tower, and a man in the window, and I am a very long way off. Pebble sits very still beside her, his red ribbon coiled in his arms like a sleeping snake.

When Jian has finished explaining, Veyra Thann speaks first.

It is a bargain, she says. It is a bad one. It is also the only one the Loom offers.

"I know."

A year of Madam Yue's life for the chance that she will live beyond the Door.

"Not to live," says Yue. "To live differently. To be a woman whose thread did not end in the same hour as a friend's."

That is a very fine distinction.

"It's the only one I've got."

Veyra's hood tilts. Then you have decided.

"I haven't decided anything."

"You have," says Hua, quietly.

They all turn.

The Warden has not moved. She sits with her hands folded over the end of her ribbon, her small clever face pale in the silver light. She is not looking at Yue. She is looking at Jian.

"She has," Hua says. "She decided in the first minute. She's been looking for a reason to say no. She hasn't found one." A faint, wry smile. "You can see it in her hands."

Yue looks down.

Her right hand is resting on the boards, and the fingers have closed, loosely, around a pair of small bright shears. They are plain, old, black-handled, with a blade the length of a finger. Tamsin has put them there. Jian had not seen her do it.

"I didn't ask for these," says Yue.

"No," says the Keeper, from the dark. Her voice is mild. "I only left them where you might find them."

Yue stares at the shears.

"Master," says Pebble.

His voice is thin and cracked. He has risen to his knees, with the red ribbon clutched against his chest, and his shaven head is gleaming with sweat. "Master, please. I saw the room. I saw you on the floor. If you cut it, you'll be—you'll be a year shorter. You'll be closer to—"

"Closer to what?"

"To the end."

"I'm already close to the end, Pebble." Yue's voice is dry and kind. "We all are. It's only a question of how we spend what's left." She looks at him. "You wove a thread that outlives the Door. Do you know what that means?"

"No."

"Neither do I." A small, tired smile. "But I think it means someone has to be there afterward. Someone who knows what happened. Someone who can say, this is what it cost." She lays her stone hand briefly on his shaven head. "I'd like it to be you. And I'd like you not to be alone."

Pebble's face crumples.

"That's not fair," he whispers.

"No," says Yue. "It never is."

For a long time she does not speak. The kettle ticks. The far clatter of the looms goes on and on, a million hands in a million rooms, passing a million shuttles through a million threads. Jian sits very still, with his hands on his knees and his steady heart beating against his ribs like a bird.

Don't, he thinks. Please don't.

Don't what?

It is Yue's voice, in his head, dry and quiet and entirely clear. He had not known the mark could carry that. He had not known she could hear him.

Don't make it easy for me, she says. Don't make it an act of sacrifice. I'm not doing this for you. A pause. I'm doing it because I've decided I'd rather be alive at the end of it than dead beside a friend. That's all. It's a selfish reason. I'd like you to know that.

Yue.

I'd also like to say I'm sorry. The thought is oddly gentle. For all the times I was angry. It was a waste.

She stands.

The shears hang from her fingers, bright in the silver light. She looks at the two threads where they lie on the table, side by side: a ribbon of gray-blue and silver, a ribbon of dark gold. They are not touching. But Jian can see, now, if he looks closely, a fine bright strand running between them, a hair's breadth thick, like the line of a spider's web.

"Where do I cut?" says Yue.

"Anywhere along it," says Tamsin. "It will take the year from the place you choose."

"Then I'll choose the middle."

She raises the shears.

Pebble makes a small sound. Hua has put her hand over her mouth. And Veyra Thann, standing at the edge of the circle with her ruined hand pressed against her chest, whispers something under her breath that might be a name, and might be a prayer.

Pebble has covered his face. Hua has drawn her knees up and wrapped both arms around them, as a child does in a thunderstorm. Even Tamsin, in the shadow of the beam, has turned her sewn eyes away, and the old hands that hold her staff are white at the knuckle.

Jian does not look away. He has made himself a promise, in the long hours at the loom: that whatever she does, he will watch it, and not flinch, and not speak. It is the one gift he has left to give. He sits with his steady hands on his knees and his heart beating hard against his ribs, and he looks at the bright strand between the two ribbons, and at the blades hovering above it, and at the face of the woman who holds them, which is calm, and set, and very young.

The blades close.
